facts.title: Most Famous Punk Rock Hotel Room Death (October 12, 1978)
facts.body: The death of Nancy Spungen at the Chelsea Hotel on October 12, 1978, is considered "probably the most famous punk rock hotel room death of them all." "And then there's probably the most famous punk rock hotel room death of them all."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Infamous Hotels and Hotel Rooms
facts.name: Punk Rock

facts.title: Soviet Awareness and Interception (1978)
facts.body: Soviet authorities became aware of punk rock in 1978 when bootleg tapes and news from legally intercepted BBC broadcasts began "dripping through the iron curtain." The KGB was conscious of this new music and its potential for social disruption and youth anger. "Soviet authorities first became aware of punk in 1978 when bootleg tapes and news were legally intercepted BBC broadcasts, started dripping through the iron curtain."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Great KGB Punk Conspiracy
facts.name: Punk Rock

facts.title: Counterculture Development (1978-79)
facts.body: During the "winter of discontent" (1978-79), exacerbated by widespread strikes and extreme cold, punk rock intensified, transforming "from being this innocuous sort of thing into a genuine counterculture." "All this simply increased the heat of punk. It went from being this innocuous sort of thing into a genuine counterculture."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Why Punk Happened
facts.name: Punk Rock

facts.title: Disastrous American Tour and Final Performance (1978)
facts.body: The Sex Pistols' American tour culminated in their final performance at the Winterland Ballroom in San Francisco on January 14, 1978. The tour was marred by hostile audiences, Sid Vicious's extreme intoxication and altercations, Malcolm McLaren's difficult management, and deep internal animosity, all of which were captured in the film "The Great Rock and Roll Swindle." This show marked the last time the original lineup would perform together for nearly 18 years, and the final appearance with Sid Vicious before his death 13 months later. "It shows a band at the end of their rope and literally ready to blow apart."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Disputes with Manager Malcolm McLaren (1978)
facts.body: As the Sex Pistols gained fame, members, particularly singer Johnny Rotten, grew suspicious of Malcolm McLaren, accusing him of mismanagement of "everything, really." The band frequently found that there was no money available when they wanted to get paid. This deteriorating relationship culminated in the band's implosion at the end of a disastrous American tour in 1978.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Mighty Managers of Rock
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Litigation and Control (1978-1987)
facts.body: Following the Sex Pistols' implosion in 1978, years of litigation ensued involving the band members and Malcolm McLaren's management company, Glitter Best. It took until 1987, nearly a decade after their breakup, for the Sex Pistols to finally wrestle away control of their music from McLaren.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Mighty Managers of Rock
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Disastrous American Tour – Deep South, 1978
facts.body: Manager Malcolm McLaren planned for the Sex Pistols' first American tour to go through the "deep conservative South" in an attempt to be subversive. The tour proved to be a disaster, marked by Sid Vicious's uncontrollable behavior and the band's self-destruction. "Manager Malcolm McLaren thought it would be really subversive if the pistols first tour of America was through the deep self."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Sid Vicious
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Band Breakup – January 14, 1978, San Francisco
facts.body: The Sex Pistols broke up hours after their final show with Sid Vicious at the Wintergarden Ballroom in San Francisco on January 14, 1978. The atmosphere within the band had become too violent, self-destructive, and strange to continue. "Hours after the show in San Francisco on January 14th 1978, the Sex Pistols broke up."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Sid Vicious
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Hostile Dallas Concert (1978)
facts.body: At the Longhorn Ballroom in Dallas on January 10, 1978, the band faced an extremely hostile crowd that pelted them with not just cans and bottles, but also rotten tomatoes and pig snouts, while Sid Vicious was notably headbutted during the performance. "The band was pelted with cans and bottles, and not just cans and bottles, because the crowd came prepared with rotten tomatoes and get this pig snouts."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Stupid History: The Music Version 1
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Disastrous American Tour – January 1978
facts.body: Manager Malcolm McLaren's plan to "conquer America" with the Sex Pistols resulted in one of rock history's most disastrous road trips. Initially, the group's visa applications were denied, forcing them to cancel an important appearance on Saturday Night Live, where Elvis Costello was called in as a last-minute replacement. The drummer for Elvis Costello's performance notably wore a t-shirt that read "Thanks, milk," a sarcastic jab at Malcolm McLaren. McLaren made a bizarre miscalculation about American culture by routing the tour away from major cities and through the deep South, an area not receptive to punk rock values. "Instead, what he got was one of the most disastrous road trips in the history of rock."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 5
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Final Concert – January 14, 1978
facts.body: The band's last show took place at the Winterland Ballroom on January 14, 1978. A recording from that night's last song captured "the sound of a band dying violently on stage." Johnny Rotten concluded the performance with the memorable line, "Ah ha ha, have I get the feeling you've been cheated? Good night." "The last show was at the Winterland Ballroom on January 14, 1978."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 5
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Murder of Nancy Spungen (October 12, 1978)
facts.body: On October 12, 1978, Sid Vicious woke up in Room 100 of the Chelsea Hotel in New York City to find his girlfriend, Nancy Spungen, dead in the bathroom from a stab wound to the stomach caused by a Jaguar K-11 hunting knife. Both had been heavily under the influence of drugs, and multiple people had cycled through their room the night before. "When he awoke, Nancy was in the bathroom, dead in a pool of blood under the sink."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Explosive Breakup in North America (1978)
facts.body: The band dramatically dissolved at the conclusion of their sole North American tour on July 14, 1978, after having released only one studio album. "They exploded at the end of their one and only North American tour. This was July 14th, 1978, and this was after exactly one studio album."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Visa Problems for Saturday Night Live (December 1978)
facts.body: The Sex Pistols were booked to perform on NBC's "Saturday Night Live" in December 1978. However, they encountered visa problems, which prevented their appearance and led to Elvis Costello being booked as a last-minute replacement. "In December 1978, the Sex Pistols were booked to play this new show on NBC called Saturday Night Live. However, they ran into visa problems and were replaced at the last second on the show by this geeky guy from England named Elvis Costello."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Why Punk Happened
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Separation (1978)
facts.body: The Sex Pistols separated in 1978, shortly before the recording of Joy Division's debut album, *Unknown Pleasures*. Their separation and the subsequent formation of Public Image Ltd marked a significant shift in the punk landscape. "tenemos justo a los 6 pistols que se acaban de separar, 1978 se separaban y se refundaba a PIL, la banda que continuaría la traditora de los 6 pistols."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 2. Unknown Pleasures
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

It took until 1987, nearly a decade after their breakup, for the Sex Pistols to finally wrestle away control of their music from McLaren.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Mighty Managers of Rock
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Murder of Nancy Spungen (October 12, 1978)
facts.body: On October 12, 1978, Sid Vicious woke up in Room 100 of the Chelsea Hotel in New York City to find his girlfriend, Nancy Spungen, dead in the bathroom from a stab wound to the stomach caused by a Jaguar K-11 hunting knife. Both had been heavily under the influence of drugs, and multiple people had cycled through their room the night before. "When he awoke, Nancy was in the bathroom, dead in a pool of blood under the sink."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Separation (1978)
facts.body: The Sex Pistols separated in 1978, shortly before the recording of Joy Division's debut album, *Unknown Pleasures*. Their separation and the subsequent formation of Public Image Ltd marked a significant shift in the punk landscape. "tenemos justo a los 6 pistols que se acaban de separar, 1978 se separaban y se refundaba a PIL, la banda que continuaría la traditora de los 6 pistols."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 2. Unknown Pleasures
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Visa Problems for Saturday Night Live (December 1978)
facts.body: The Sex Pistols were booked to perform on NBC's "Saturday Night Live" in December 1978. However, they encountered visa problems, which prevented their appearance and led to Elvis Costello being booked as a last-minute replacement. "In December 1978, the Sex Pistols were booked to play this new show on NBC called Saturday Night Live. However, they ran into visa problems and were replaced at the last second on the show by this geeky guy from England named Elvis Costello."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Why Punk Happened
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Disastrous American Tour and Final Performance (1978)
facts.body: The Sex Pistols' American tour culminated in their final performance at the Winterland Ballroom in San Francisco on January 14, 1978. The tour was marred by hostile audiences, Sid Vicious's extreme intoxication and altercations, Malcolm McLaren's difficult management, and deep internal animosity, all of which were captured in the film "The Great Rock and Roll Swindle." This show marked the last time the original lineup would perform together for nearly 18 years, and the final appearance with Sid Vicious before his death 13 months later. "It shows a band at the end of their rope and literally ready to blow apart."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Name Change from Warsaw to Joy Division (1978)
facts.body: When their debut EP was made, the band was still using their original name, Warsaw. However, by the time the record was released in June 1978, they had adopted the name Joy Division. "At the time this record was made, Joy Division was still going by their original name, which was Warsaw, but by the time the record came out, they adopted Joy Division."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Valuable Vinyl
facts.name: Joy Division

facts.title: RCA Contract and Disillusionment (1978)
facts.body: In 1978, Joy Division signed with RCA, which offered a significant budget and good producers. However, the collaboration was a failure as RCA attempted to mold them into a prefabricated punk product, leading to the band's discomfort with the sound. They ultimately abandoned the label in the summer of 1978. "Durante 1978 los JVS empiezan a trabajar en los estudios de la RCA con bastante presupuesto y además con bastantes buenos productores y acaba siendo un fracaso."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 1. Inicios en la escena post-punk
facts.name: Joy Division

facts.title: Signing with Factory Records (Late 1978)
facts.body: After leaving RCA, Joy Division connected with Tony Wilson in Manchester, who signed them to his newly founded Factory Records. Although not technically the label's first release, Joy Division's work became Factory Records' first relevant project, effectively launching the label. "Factory records prácticamente se estrenan, aunque físicamente no es técnicamente el primer trabajo que hace factor y records, el primer trabajo relevante que haces es la yoidivisión."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 1. Inicios en la escena post-punk
facts.name: Joy Division

facts.title: Early Local Success and Influences (Summer 1978)
facts.body: By the summer of 1978, Joy Division was regularly performing concerts in Manchester, benefiting from Tony Wilson's influence. They had built a loyal local fanbase and were already developing a clear sound distinct from pure punk, incorporating influences from bands like Cabaret Voltaire, Pink Floyd, and Can. "En el verano de 1978 yoidivisión ya daba concertos con bastante regularidad en Manchester, gracias a la influencia de Tony Wilson."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 1. Inicios en la escena post-punk
facts.name: Joy Division

facts.title: Market Evolution (1978-1981)
facts.body: The musical market in the United Kingdom between 1978 and 1981 underwent significant changes, which influenced the evolution of the band members. "Y el mercado musical del reino nido en el 78 en el 81 no tenía nada que ver."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 4. La banda tras el final
facts.name: Joy Division

facts.body: Under Rob Gretton's management, Joy Division signed with Factory Records, a "very cool, new indie label." Gretton's influence extended beyond Joy Division, as he also helped sign other bands, including Happy Mondays and OMD, to the label.

facts.title: Pre-1978 Categorization
facts.body: R&B was one of the four straightforward categories for popular music before 1978, alongside rock, pop, and country. "Before 1978, things were fairly simple...We had rock, we had pop, we had country, we had R&B."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave
facts.name: r&b

facts.title: Post-1978 Bifurcation and Mutation
facts.body: After 1978, R&B underwent a significant bifurcation into classic and modern styles, with its main sounds, including funk and soul, mutating rapidly to encompass disco and, within a year, hip hop. "R&B's main sounds, which included fun console, began mutating even faster, expanding to include disco, and within a year, hip hop."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave
facts.name: r&b

facts.title: Poor Record Deal and Management Change (1978)
facts.body: Bernie Rhodes negotiated a "very poor record deal" for The Clash, which led the band to turn against him. Consequently, Rhodes was out as their manager in 1978 and was replaced by Carolyn Coon, a painter and rock journalist.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Mighty Managers of Rock
facts.name: The Clash

facts.title: Mick Jones in Sid Vicious's New York Band – September 1978
facts.body: Mick Jones, guitarist for The Clash, joined Sid Vicious's temporary band for three shows at Max's Kansas City in New York in September 1978. "He had a band together, consisting of two guys from the New York Dolls and Mick Jones of the Clash."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Sid Vicious
facts.name: The Clash

facts.title: "Cleansing Dervish" and "Shock Treatment" Description (1978)
facts.body: Gary Mullenx, writing for the Morning News in Wilmington, Delaware in 1978, provided an evocative description of heavy metal, stating it "swirls through the mind like a cleansing dervish and wrenches the gut like a good shock treatment." This highlights the genre's intense, cathartic, and physically impactful effect on listeners. "quote, swirls through the mind like a cleansing dervish and wrenches the gut like a good shock treatment."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal
facts.name: Heavy Metal

facts.title: 1978-1982 Music Industry Revolution
facts.body: Between 1978 and 1982, the music industry underwent a revolution, characterized by the emergence of new forms of heavy metal. "nacían nuevas maneras de heavy metal"
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.title: Emergence from Punk Burnout (Late 1978)
facts.body: By late 1978, the initial punk rock scene and its distinct sound began to wane. A new wave of underground music emerged that, while recognizing punk's influence, deviated significantly in sound, arrangements, instrumentation, fashion, and politics from bands like The Ramones and Sex Pistols, necessitating new descriptive terminology. "But by late 1978 the original punk rock scene in sound was beginning to burn out."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Etymology: Part 1
facts.name: Post-Punk

facts.title: Early Terminology Attempts (1978-1979)
facts.body: As the original punk rock scene declined, writers sought new ways to categorize the evolving music. John Savage proposed "new music" (with a K) in late 1978, while Simon Frith tried to popularize "after punk" (one word) in spring 1979, but neither term successfully captured public imagination. "As the original punk rock scene ran down a number of people offered up new words. There was new music spelled with a K on the end."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Etymology: Part 1
facts.name: Post-Punk

facts.title: First Print Usage (February 1978)
facts.body: The phrase "post punk" first appeared in print in an article in the UK's NME magazine in February 1978, authored by Charles Shaar Murray. Paul Morley later adopted the term, integrating it into his reviews starting in 1980, which contributed to its broader acceptance. "The first time anybody can remember the phrase post punk being used in print was an article in the UK's NME magazine written by Charles Schar Murray in February of 1978."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Etymology: Part 1
facts.name: Post-Punk

facts.title: Era Definition (1978-mid 80s)
facts.body: The post-punk era, roughly spanning from 1978 to the mid-1980s, is characterized by sounds and styles that, while not punk, could not have existed without punk's initial impact, forming the foundation for the alternative revolution of the 1990s. "We now call this the post punk era. And this period of time, roughly from 1978 through to the middle 80s, created the foundations for the alternative revolution in the 90s and beyond."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave
facts.name: Post-Punk

facts.title: 1978-1982 Music Industry Revolution
facts.body: Between 1978 and 1982, the music industry underwent a revolution, seeing the birth of post-punk. "nacían el post-punk"
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Cómo Michael Jackson hizo el disco más vendido de la historia
facts.name: Post-Punk

facts.title: Polarizing Force (1978)
facts.body: In 1978, disco was an intensely polarizing force in music, compelling fans to gravitate away from mainstream sounds and towards the expanding fringes of popular music. It was profoundly hated by rock fans, who condemned it as "evil, vacuous, boring, mindless, empty and obnoxious." "That repulsive force, that dark matter was known as disco."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 6
facts.name: Disco

facts.title: 1978-1982 Music Industry Revolution
facts.body: Between 1978 and 1982, the music industry underwent a significant revolution, during which disco music experienced a rapid decline. This period was characterized by the emergence of new musical styles. "la música disco, la calle en picado"
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Cómo Michael Jackson hizo el disco más vendido de la historia
facts.name: Disco

facts.title: Peak Influence in 1978
facts.body: By 1978, disco music had reached its peak, exerting a significant influence across the music industry. The Rolling Stones, for instance, incorporated disco elements into their "Some Girls" album. "la música disco ya estaba por todo lo alto."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: The Rolling Stones: Some Girls y su portada llena de demandas.
facts.name: Disco

facts.title: Peak Influence in 1978
facts.body: By 1978, disco music had reached its peak, exerting a significant influence across the music industry. The Rolling Stones, for instance, incorporated disco elements into their "Some Girls" album. "la música disco ya estaba por todo lo alto."

facts.title: Drug-Induced Incidents on American Tour (1978)
facts.body: During the Sex Pistols' ill-fated American tour, Sid Vicious frequently became so heavily intoxicated that he was physically assaulted by his own bodyguard. These incidents underscored the chaotic and dysfunctional nature of the tour, contributing to the overall animosity within the band. "Sid Vicious kept getting so wasted that he managed to get beat up by his own bodyguard."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5
facts.name: Sid Vicious

facts.title: Nancy Spungen's Death (1978)
facts.body: On October 12, 1978, Sid Vicious awoke from a heroin haze to discover his girlfriend, Nancy Spungen, dead from stab wounds in the bathroom of their room at the Chelsea Hotel in New York, with his knife found in her stomach. The exact circumstances of her death—whether it was murder, suicide, or a drug deal gone wrong—remain unknown.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9
facts.name: Sid Vicious

facts.title: Involvement in Nancy Spungen's Death (October 12, 1978)
facts.body: Sid Vicious, bassist for the Sex Pistols, was implicated in the death of his girlfriend, Nancy Spungen, who was found stabbed to death in room 100 of the Chelsea Hotel in New York on October 12, 1978. Sid and Nancy were both heroin and Tuinal addicts, and on the night of her death, Sid reportedly took up to 52 Tuinal tablets, which would have rendered him unconscious. Although he initially confessed, his level of incapacitation made it unlikely he remembered. He was arrested and charged with Nancy's murder but died of a heroin overdose before the trial could commence. "Sid was arrested, charged with Nancy's murder, and then died of a heroin overdose before things could go to trial."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Infamous Hotels and Hotel Rooms
facts.name: Sid Vicious

facts.title: Nancy Spungen's Death - October 12, 1978
facts.body: His girlfriend, Nancy Spungen, was found dead under the bathroom sink of room 100 at the Chelsea Hotel in New York on the morning of October 12, 1978, having been stabbed in the stomach with a knife owned by Sid. "She was found dead under the bathroom sink of room 100 of the Chelsea Hotel in New York on the morning of October the 12th of 1978. She had been stabbed in the stomach by a big knife, a knife owned by Sid."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Murder!
facts.name: Sid Vicious

facts.title: Disappearance and Overdose After Breakup – January 1978
facts.body: Hours after the Sex Pistols broke up on January 14, 1978, Sid disappeared until he was found comatose in a closet in the Haight-Ashbury district. While attempting to fly back to London, he managed to overdose on the plane during a connection in New York. "He disappeared until someone found him comatose in a closet somewhere in the high-dashberry district."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Sid Vicious
facts.name: Sid Vicious

facts.title: Move to New York City – August 1978
facts.body: With nowhere to go after their eviction, Sid and Nancy decided to move to New York City in August 1978, a place where Nancy claimed to know people. This move was partly funded by a £10,000 loan from Malcolm McLaren. "With nowhere to go, they decided that it was time to move to New York."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Sid Vicious
facts.name: Sid Vicious

facts.title: Nancy Spungen's Murder – October 12, 1978
facts.body: On the morning of October 12, 1978, Nancy Spungen was found dead in the bathroom of room 100 at the Chelsea Hotel, stabbed in the stomach with a 007 brand knife. Sid claimed to have no memory of the event, as he had passed out after taking 22 Tuinals. "Nancy was lying dead on the bathroom floor of the hotel room. She had been stabbed in the stomach and had blood to death."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Sid Vicious
facts.name: Sid Vicious

facts.title: Arrested for Second-Degree Murder – October 13, 1978
facts.body: Sid Vicious was charged with second-degree murder for Nancy Spungen's death on October 13, 1978, and sent to the detox unit at Rikers Island Prison. Bail was set at $50,000. "Sid was charged with second-degree murder and sent to the detox unit at Rikers Island Prison."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Sid Vicious
facts.name: Sid Vicious

facts.title: Malcolm McLaren Posts Bail – October 17, 1978
facts.body: Malcolm McLaren posted Sid's $50,000 bail, leading to his release from Rikers Island on October 17, 1978. "October 17, 1978. Malcolm McLaren posts Sid's bail and he's released."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Sid Vicious
facts.name: Sid Vicious

facts.title: Assault on Patti Smith's Brother – December 9, 1978
facts.body: On December 9, 1978, Sid got into a fight with the brother of singer Patti Smith during a night out and slashed his face with a beer bottle. He was arrested on felony assault charges and sent back to Rikers Island. "They get into a fight and Sid slashes the guy's face with a beer bottle."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Sid Vicious
facts.name: Sid Vicious

facts.title: Hunting for Punk-like Bands (1978)
facts.body: In 1978, RCA and other record labels were aggressively seeking out bands that emulated the Sex Pistols' punk sound or played verbally aggressive music, viewing it as a highly profitable market. "tanto la RCA, pues como muchas otras discográficas estaban comentivamente a la caza de cualquier grupo que pudiesen echar un poco más mercado que diez, un poco ese aire pan de los expuestos."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 1. Inicios en la escena post-punk
facts.name: RCA Records

facts.title: Failed Collaboration with Joy Division (1978)
facts.body: RCA signed Joy Division in 1978, providing a substantial budget and good producers. However, the label's attempt to create a "prefabricated product" aligning with the punk trend clashed with the band's desire for new sounds, leading to a failed collaboration and Joy Division abandoning the label. "Durante 1978 los JVS empiezan a trabajar en los estudios de la RCA con bastante presupuesto y además con bastantes buenos productores y acaba siendo un fracaso."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 1. Inicios en la escena post-punk

facts.title: Parallel Foundation and Early Careers (1978-1979)
facts.body: Sonic Youth and Swans were founded simultaneously in 1978-79, knew each other, were friends, and released their first albums in the same year, indicating very parallel trajectories in their early stages. "Justo en 1978, 79 al mismo tiempo que estaba saliendo ese recopilatorio se estaba fundando las dos bandas, Suansi y Sonichuth tienen una vida muy paralela porque se fundaron a la vez, se conocían, eran amigos, sacan sus primeras discos en el mismo año, entonces son dos bandas que tuvieron vidas muy paralelas en sus inicios."

facts.title: Saturday Night Live Incident (December 17, 1978)
facts.body: As a last-minute replacement for the Sex Pistols (who faced visa issues), Elvis Costello appeared on "Saturday Night Live" in December 1978. Producers explicitly asked him not to play "Radio Radio" due to NBC's ownership of radio stations and the song's critical lyrics. Costello agreed but then famously played "Radio Radio" instead of the requested song, causing a stir. "But then this is what happened on December 17, 1978... Radio Radio."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Why Punk Happened
facts.name: Elvis Costello

facts.title: Wrigley's Spearmint Gum Commercial (1978)
facts.body: In 1978, facing financial constraints, all three members of The Police agreed to appear in a television commercial for Wrigley's Spearmint Gum, a concept that required them to bleach their hair a striking white blonde. "And that's why in 1978, they agreed to appear in a TV commercial for Riggley's Spiriment Gum."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.name: The Police

facts.title: US Tour and CBGB Debut (1978)
facts.body: In October 1978, Miles Copeland self-funded a tour of America for The Police, commencing in New York City. Their first performance was at the punk mecca CBGB, where they delivered an acclaimed, punk-worthy set at the notoriously grungy but hip club. "Miles Copeland had the clever idea to self-fund a tour of America for the police, starting in New York City. When they arrived in October of 78, their first stop was Punk Mecca CBGB. At the notoriously grungy but reliably hip club, the police played an acclaimed punk-worthy set."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: If You Love Sting, Set Him Free Edition Part 1

facts.title: Post-Berlin Trilogy Prolificacy (1978-1980s)
facts.body: After the Berlin Trilogy, Brian Eno returned to Düsseldorf and became extremely prolific between 1978 and the 1980s, deepening his interest in World Music and producing many important artists, including Talking Heads. "La rafiro Braianno entre el 78 y el 80 y pico hizo un montón de cosas, aparte de esos discos, así interesó también muchísimo por el World Music."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 3
facts.name: Brian Eno

facts.title: Coined the Term "Ambient" (1978)
facts.body: Brian Eno coined the term "ambient" with the release of his 1978 album, "Music for Airports." This work laid the foundational philosophy for the genre. "Al fin de al cabo, él había coñado el término ambient en su disco Music for I report, en 1978."
facts.source: Central Sonora
facts.episode: Por Qué Tu Cerebro Nunca Olvidará Este Sonido
facts.name: Brian Eno

facts.title: Philosophy on Music (1978)
facts.body: In his 1978 album "Music for Airports," Eno articulated his philosophy that music should be "as ignorable as it is interesting." This concept proved to be ideal for the background atmosphere required by the operating system of the future, Windows 95. "En este disco, y no defendía que la música debía ser tan ignorable como interesante."
facts.source: Central Sonora
facts.episode: Por Qué Tu Cerebro Nunca Olvidará Este Sonido
facts.name: Brian Eno

facts.title: Casting for Grease (1978)
facts.body: Casting director John Thurm had Olivia Newton-John in mind for the role of Sandy, but she had doubts due to being older than John Travolta and requested a screen test to assess their chemistry, despite it not being a requirement. Ultimately, her portrayal became iconic. "She wanted to see though if she had any chemistry at all with John Travolta, especially since she was older than he was."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 40 - Honestly Loving Olivia Newton-John
facts.name: Olivia Newton-John

facts.title: Critic's Harsh Review of Grease (1978)
facts.body: Cliff Radell, a 20-year-old pop critic for the Cincinnati Enquirer, penned a highly critical review of *Grease*, titled "If It Smells, It Must Be Greece." He disparaged Olivia Newton-John's performance, calling her a "Mousy Voiced, Dishwashed, Blonde Actress who can't act, can't sing, can't dance, and can't pass for 36, much less, 16." He also lambasted John Travolta's performance in the same review. "Greece is Olivia Newton-John's first American film. I hope it is her last."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 40 - Honestly Loving Olivia Newton-John
facts.name: Olivia Newton-John

facts.title: Role in "Grease" (1978)
facts.body: Olivia Newton-John starred in the film "Grease" in the summer of 1978, where her voice was featured through the character of Sandy. "when my cousins took me to the movies to see Greece for the first time, I was six going on seven, Newton-John was basically my first pop star crush, or at least Sandy was."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.title: CBGB Staple (1978)
facts.body: By 1978, Blondie was a staple at CBGB in New York and accepted by all the punks. While their music was not purely punk, it could not have been created without punk's prior existence, as it adopted the correct attitude and approach but introduced additional elements that defined the New Wave sound. "By 1978, was a staple at CBGB in New York, they were accepted by all the punks."

facts.title: Exploration of Hip-Hop with Fab 5 Freddy (1978)
facts.body: In 1978, Debbie Harry and Chris Stein were introduced to the emerging hip-hop scene in the Bronx by Fred Brathwaite, also known as Fab 5 Freddy, whom they met at CBGB. Freddy saw a synergy between the downtown punk and uptown hip-hop scenes, leading Harry and Stein to experiment with rap, starting with an unreleased Christmas record and culminating in "Rapture." "The story goes that in 1978, Debbie Harry and Chris Stein were taken by Fred Brathwaite, better known in hip-hop circles as Fab5 Freddie. Up to the Bronx, where they witnessed their first rap show..."

facts.title: Jazz (1978) - Bicycle Race Nudism Controversy
facts.body: The iconography surrounding the first single "Bicycle Race" was highly controversial. Freddie Mercury, inspired by a photograph of nude women in a race, wanted to base the single and album's visual theme on this. Due to censorship, the single cover could not show full nudity, so a small cropped image of a nude woman on a bicycle had panties drawn onto her. The original "Jazz" album versions included a small poster of the nude women's race, which was censored in countries like the United States, forcing Queen to remove it. To circumvent this, a coupon was included, allowing fans to mail away for the poster. Queen subsequently created extensive iconography around the nude cyclists, including posters, concert visuals, and merchandise. This visual theme was significant in the 1970s, an era when nudism was a form of protest against the connection between nudity and sexuality. "Esta fotografía, acabo siendo censurada en muchos países como Estados Unidos donde no podía mandarse fotos de desnudo."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: QUEEN como iconografía estética y gráfica
facts.name: Queen

facts.title: "Satanic" Branding Strategy (1978)
facts.body: In 1978, eight years after establishing a consistent following, Ozzy Osbourne clarified that Black Sabbath was not a satanic band. He stated their dark imagery and themes were a deliberate strategy to "create a brand to sell the band," indicating a calculated marketing approach rather than genuine occult beliefs. "In 1978, Ozzy Osborne said that black Sabbath was not a satanic band, and that they were really just trying to quote, create a brand to sell the band."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal
facts.name: Black Sabbath

facts.title: NTSB Investigation Findings (June 1978)
facts.body: Eight months after the crash, in June 1978, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) ruled the probable cause of the accident as "fuel exhaustion and a total loss of power from both engines due to crew inattention to fuel supply." The report stated that the crew was "either negligent or ignorant of the increased fuel consumption because they failed to monitor adequately the engine instruments for fuel flow and fuel quantity." "The National Transportation Safety Board looked into things. And eight months later, in June 1978, it ruled that the probable cause of the accident was fuel exhaustion and a total loss of power from both engines due to crew inattention to fuel supply."

facts.title: NTSB Investigation Findings (June 1978)
facts.body: Eight months after the crash, in June 1978, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) ruled the probable cause of the accident as "fuel exhaustion and a total loss of power from both engines due to crew inattention to fuel supply." The report stated that the crew was "either negligent or ignorant of the increased fuel consumption because they failed to monitor adequately the engine instruments for fuel flow and fuel quantity." "The National Transportation Safety Board looked into things. And eight months later, in June 1978, it ruled that the probable cause of the accident was fuel exhaustion and a total loss of power from both engines due to crew inattention to fuel supply."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Awful Concert Sound (1978)
facts.body: The concert in Winnipeg Arena on August 30, 1978, featured Aerosmith as the headliner and ACDC as the opener. The sound was extremely poor, described as a "blare of distortion" for over two and a half hours, making it impossible to recognize any of Aerosmith's songs. "People around me were going, are they playing Walk This Way or is that Walk in the Dog? I can't tell."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Financial Struggles and Pin Floyd's Support (1978)
facts.body: By 1978, Sid Baret, despite having earned substantial money from Pin Floyd and ongoing royalties from their first two albums, ran out of money while living in London. He moved back to Cambridge to live with his family. Pin Floyd made several gestures, including re-editions and securing rights, to ensure he continued to receive royalties as a full member (even for works where he contributed minimally, like the second album). This financial support allowed him and his family to live comfortably without money worries for the rest of his life. "La banda tenía un último gesto hacia el artista para ayudar a generar un poco más de dinero y que pudiese acabar en paz y sin problemas económicos al resto de sus días."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Pink Floyd: Tras los pasos de Syd Barrett
facts.name: Syd Barrett

facts.title: Term Coined by Brian Eno (1978)
facts.body: The genre term "ambient" was explicitly coined by Brian Eno with the release of his album "Music for Airports" in 1978, establishing its definition and purpose within the musical landscape. "él había coñado el término ambient en su disco Music for I report, en 1978."

facts.title: Eno's Philosophy: Ignorable Yet Interesting (1978)
facts.body: Brian Eno's core philosophy for ambient music, as articulated with "Music for Airports," was that it should be "as ignorable as it is interesting." This duality allowed the music to exist unobtrusively in the background while still offering engaging details upon focused listening. "la música debía ser tan ignorable como interesante."

facts.title: Robert Hilburn's Criticism (1978)
facts.body: In a 1978 review of Manilow's Greek Theater concert in Los Angeles, critic Robert Hilburn predictably dismissed the performance as "plain and bland." However, Hilburn also suggested that Manilow "was the beneficiary of the public's renewed fondness for simple, unprobing artists." "Robert Hillburn wrote a review of the opening night of a seven-night run of Manelow concerts at the Greek theater in Los Angeles in 1978, and predictably said it was plain and bland and blah, blah, blah, blah."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 34 - A 70s Pop Manifesto - Finding Meaning in 70s Pop
facts.name: Barry Manilow

facts.title: First US Performance (1978)
facts.body: Triumph's inaugural performance in America took place in San Antonio in 1978, drawing an audience of approximately 6,000 people, which constituted their largest crowd up to that point. "Their first performance in America was in front of about 6,000 people in San Antonio in 1978, which was their largest crowd to date."

facts.title: Formation (1978)
facts.body: Mute Records was one of three important independent labels, alongside Factory Records and Rough Trade, that began releasing material in 1978. These labels emerged with non-commercial aims after the punk revolution opened doors for riskier music. facts.title: The Rheostatics Formation and Influence (1978)
facts.body: Formed in Toronto in 1978, The Rheostatics befriended The Tragically Hip in the 80s and 90s. Despite not being commercially focused, their unconventional and eclectic approach to rock garnered critical praise and significant influence. "Their history goes back to 1978 in Toronto. They became friends with the tragically hip through the 80s and 90s and they were never exactly commercial sounding but their unconventional and eclectic approach to rock made them beloved by critics and very influential in certain places."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Lost CanRock Bands of the 90s: Part 2
facts.name: The Rheostatics

facts.title: The Rheostatics Active Periods and Reunions (1978-2007, 2015-Present)
facts.body: The band had an initial run from 1978 to 2007, followed by a brief reunion. Since 2015, they have been performing occasional gigs together. "The Rio's initial run was from 78 to 2007. There was a brief reunion and since 2015 they played the occasional gig together."
